newsitem.title: USA: LeBow seeks tobacco pact with secret papers.
newsitem.headline: LeBow seeks tobacco pact with secret papers.

text.p: Brooke Group Ltd. Chairman Bennett LeBow is seeking a settlement with the states suing the tobacco industry in a deal that could involve the exchange of confidential documents, legal sources said Thursday.

Brooke is the parent of Liggett Group Inc., the first tobacco company to ever settle cigarette lawsuits. Liggett shocked the industry and the financial community in March 1996 when it reached an accord with five states that had sued cigarette makers to recoup the health care costs of smokers.

However, 18 state attorneys general have now filed such lawsuits, as well as the lieutenant governor of Alabama. New York City, San Francisco, Los Angeles County and San Jose, Calif., have also joined in the battle.

LeBow's negotiations come when some state attorneys general and some plaintiffs lawyers are seeking a possible legislative solution to the mounting litigation against the cigarette makers. The group has met with intermediaries who have contacts in the tobacco industry. So far, cigarette companies have denied any participation in the talks.

Legal sources said LeBow wants to reach an accord that would settle all or most of the Medicaid lawsuits and that as part of any such deal he would offer to turn over potentially damaging documents about the tobacco industry.
A LeBow spokesman would not comment. Liggett previously reached pacts with Mississippi, Florida, Massachusetts, West Virginia and Louisiana.

"We have had extensive negotiations over a long period of time in various parts of the country, but no agreement has been reached," said Don Barrett, a Mississippi lawyer who represents a number of the states that have sued, including Arizona, Washington and Illinois.
"If an agreement is reached, it would be with all or most of those states (that have sued)," Barrett said. He added that lawyers for some of the cities and counties are also involved in the talks.
Barrett would not discuss details of the talks, but other sources said LeBow has offered to turn over internal documents that could be damaging to the industry.

Minnesota Attorney General Hubert Humphrey III, whose state rejected last year's settlement with Liggett, said the tobacco industry has produced about 28 million pages of documents in the Minnesota litigation.
"The issue for Minnesota is whether Liggett can produce any additional information we haven't already uncovered. I am open to all legal means of learning the truth," Humphrey said.
The Wall Street Journal reported Thursday that some of the documents could involve notes of meetings held by a group of top in-house lawyers from the the nation's leading tobacco companies.

Clifford Douglas, an Evanston, Ill., consultant to plaintiffs' lawyers suing the tobacco industry, said if such documents were turned over, they might reveal information about legal strategies that has been difficult to obtain.

"It could be pretty explosive in strengthening the plaintiffs' weaponry," he said. "If it can be shown that industry lawyers facilitiated wrongful conduct and hiding critical information from the public and government officials, then the defendants' could find themselves up against the wall."
The first of the Medicaid cases, filed by Mississippi, is scheduled to go to trial on June 2.
R.J. Reynolds Tobacco, a unit of RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp., said it would be impossible for it to speculate about the documents without having seen any firm agreement.

"It sounds as if there's yet another illusory 'settlement' in the making, the greatest value of which will be to provide fodder for plaintiff lawyers to attempt to legitimise lawsuits which have no basis in fact or law -- that is nothing more than a public relations ploy," the company said.
